title: A centralized privacy request can scale consumer control while leaving broker-level deletion unresolved
source_unit: California Privacy Protection Agency public explanation of the Delete Request and Opt-out Platform (DROP)
geography: California consumers and registered data brokers

denominator.unit: consumers reported by CalPrivacy as having signed up and submitted deletion requests; approximate lower-bound wording

data_broker_coverage.unit: over 600 active data brokers covered by one request

consumer_request.value: one request to delete personal information and stop sale

raw_data_storage.value: DROP hashes entered information and says raw data is not stored or shared with brokers

status_visibility.value: deleted, exempted, opted out of sale, not found, or pending

broker_response_deadline.unit: days after a matched request, subject to exemptions

verified_deletion_and_lived_outcome.unit: missing consumer-level completion, residual exposure, trust, switching, or wellbeing outcome

observations.method: Official California Privacy Protection Agency implementation explanation; participation, system scope, privacy-by-design, status categories, and response timing are retained separately from matched deletion, exemption, residual data, and downstream consumer outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: The public page reports submissions and the designed status route but does not provide the distribution of statuses across brokers, actual completion rates, exemptions, duplicate matching failures, re-collection, or consumer-level trust and behavior change.
observations.subgroup: California residents eligible for DROP and data brokers covered by the system; status outcomes may differ by information supplied and broker records.
observations.counterinterpretation: A centralized route can lower effort and increase consumer agency even if some records are not found or exempted; a deletion status can also reduce sale without removing the underlying data.

observations.period: August 2026 follow-up after mandatory processing began

denominator.unit: approximately California consumers registered for DROP

registered_data_brokers.unit: data brokers in the DROP system

brokers_reporting_processing.unit: approximately percent of data brokers reporting that they processed deletion requests

request_status_route.value: consumers can log in and check broker-level deletion status after processing begins

consumer_level_deletion_and_residual_exp.unit: missing broker-match, deletion, exemption, re-collection, and lived-outcome detail

observations.method: Official California Privacy Protection Agency follow-up announcement reviewed as a later implementation observation for the same DROP route.
observations.uncertainty: The agency reports registrations, broker participation, and the share reporting processing, but not the number of requests processed, status distribution, deletion completion, exemptions, record matching, repeat collection, or consumer-level privacy and trust outcomes.
observations.subgroup: California DROP registrants and registered data brokers; the reported processing share is broker-level and is not a consumer-level completion rate.
observations.counterinterpretation: A quarter of brokers reporting processing is meaningful implementation progress, but reporting activity may precede completed deletion and does not show that the remaining brokers failed to comply or that a registrant's data was removed.

observations.period: Current DROP implementation timeline checked September 21, 2026

denominator.unit: consumer deletion requests and broker-level status updates in the DROP production route

broker_processing_interval.unit: days; data brokers must access DROP at least once every 45 days to process requests

status_update_delay.unit: days; status updates may take up to 90 days to appear depending on broker workflows

status_categories.value: record deleted, record exempted, record opted out of sale, record not found, or pending

match_sensitivity.value: adding optional identifiers such as mobile advertising ID, connected-TV ID, or VIN may improve matching

verified_deletion_and_residual_exposure.unit: status visibility and processing rules do not independently prove complete deletion, exemption validity, re-collection prevention, or durable consumer control

observations.method: Official California Privacy Protection Agency DROP implementation and status-route pages reviewed as a temporal follow-up; processing cadence, status delay, outcome categories, and matching conditions are retained separately from consumer-level deletion and residual exposure.
observations.uncertainty: The public route does not disclose the distribution of statuses, how many requests remain pending beyond the stated timeline, the share of records not found or exempted, whether brokers re-collect information after deletion, or whether a consumer's status accurately describes all data held.
observations.subgroup: California DROP users and registered data brokers; status timing varies by broker workflow and information supplied by the consumer.
observations.counterinterpretation: A 90-day status window may reflect a designed processing cycle rather than institutional failure, and a not-found or opt-out-of-sale result may be correct under the data held or legal scope. Neither interpretation establishes durable privacy for the individual.

related_sources.claim: The GM/OnStar order supplies a separate product-level data-control comparison with request and deletion routes.
related_sources.access_boundary: DROP is a California multi-broker route and cannot be pooled with GM/OnStar request completion or vehicle switching.

boundary: This record establishes a large-scale centralized privacy-request route with participant volume, broker coverage, privacy-preserving intake, status categories, and response timing. It does not establish broker-level match or deletion rates, exemptions, residual data, re-collection, actual user trust, switching, wellbeing, or durable privacy. The route is an implementation and contestability stage, not a verified privacy outcome.
